record.paper_title: On some open problems of number theory
record.original_question: For a positive integer n, let s(n) be the sum of all proper divisors of n. Two positive integers m < n are amicable if s(m) = n and s(n) = m. Are there infinitely many amicable pairs?

artifact.self_contained_problem: For a positive integer $n$, let $s(n) = \sum_{d \mid n,\, d < n} d$ denote the sum of the proper divisors of $n$ (equivalently, $s(n) = \sigma(n) - n$, where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function). A pair of positive integers $(m, n)$ with $m < n$ is called an amicable pair if $s(m) = n$ and $s(n) = m$. Determine whether there exist infinitely many amicable pairs.
artifact.status_search_result: It is a long-standing open problem whether infinitely many amicable pairs exist. Although millions of amicable pairs have been computed (e.g., by Pedersen and Garcia), no proof of infinitude is known. Pomerance has shown that the set of amicable numbers has density zero and that the sum of reciprocals of amicable numbers is finite, but these results do not resolve the infinitude question.

status_evidence.title: Amicable numbers - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is not known if there are infinitely many amicable pairs.
status_evidence.claim: The existence of infinitely many amicable pairs is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Pomerance, On amicable numbers
status_evidence.snippet: The sum of the reciprocals of the amicable numbers is finite; whether there are infinitely many remains open.
status_evidence.claim: Density and reciprocal-sum results are known, but infinitude is open.
